summary: Describes a media type and method for applying patches to configuration datastores using data defined in YANG.

eli5.summary: Rather than rewriting a whole settings page, you send a short list of changes to apply.

questions: yang patch vs restconf plain patch
subtitle: A way to send RESTCONF servers an ordered list of configuration edits that all succeed or all fail together.

tldr.problem: The plain patch mechanism in RESTCONF edits one thing at a time and gives clients little control over how an edit is carried out.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends an HTTP PATCH whose body is a YANG Patch: an ordered list of edits, each with an ID, one of seven operations, a target and sometimes a value. The server applies the edits in order and returns a status report.
tldr.outcome: If any edit fails, the datastore is left unchanged, and the status response says which edit failed and why. It is a Standards Track document.

today: RFC 8072 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It defines YANG Patch only for use with RESTCONF (RFC 8040) and configuration datastores.

sections.title: Why Another Patch Format
sections.content:
NETCONF defines datastores that hold configuration described by YANG schemas. RFC 8040 lets clients edit those with RESTCONF, but its plain patch mechanism is coarse. RFC 8072 adds an ordered edit list that gives RESTCONF client developers more precise control over the edit procedure.

The RFC defines two media types, application/yang-patch+xml and application/yang-patch+json, for use with the HTTP PATCH method from RFC 5789. It specifies their use only with RESTCONF, and only for configuration datastores. Any protocol that supports the media type must apply none of the changes if the whole patch cannot be applied.
sections.eli5: The old way of changing settings was like fixing a mistake by crossing out one word at a time. This new way lets you hand over a short list of exactly which changes to make.

sections.title: Targets and Patch Basics
sections.content:
A YANG Patch is an ordered list of edits applied to the target datastore by the RESTCONF server. Compared with the plain patch of RFC 8040, it can edit several sub-resources in one PATCH, offers seven operations, and processes edits in the order the client gives, so error reports can be precise even when several errors occur.

The request URI picks the target resource. It can be the datastore resource itself (for example {+restconf}/data) or a data resource inside it (for example {+restconf}/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces). It MUST identify exactly one resource instance: more than one gets a 400 Bad Request and none gets a 404 Not Found.

Each edit then has its own target leaf. If the request URI names the datastore, that path is absolute and starts at a top-level data node, and it must not be a single /. If the request URI names a data resource, the path is relative to it, and a single / means the target resource itself.

YANG Patch can only edit data resources. It cannot replace a whole datastore the way <copy-config> can.
sections.eli5: You first say which drawer you are working in, then each item on your list says which exact thing inside that drawer to change.

sections.title: The yang-patch Request
sections.content:
The request body is a yang-patch container. It has a mandatory patch-id, an arbitrary string from the client that identifies the whole patch. Clients SHOULD try to make it unique, and servers SHOULD include it, along with the optional comment, in audit logs.

Inside is an ordered edit list. Each edit has an edit-id, an operation, a target, and optionally point, where and value. The where setting (before, after, first or last, default last) applies only to insert and move. point names the reference entry when where is before or after. The value is used only for create, merge, replace and insert.

Each edit MUST identify exactly one data resource instance. An edit that does not match an existing resource and is not create causes the request to be rejected with 404 Not Found. A server MUST return the Accept-Patch header field in an OPTIONS response so clients can learn which encodings (XML, JSON or both) it accepts.
sections.eli5: The list has a name for the whole job, and each line has its own label, an action, a place, and sometimes the new thing to put there.

sections.title: Edit Operations
sections.content:
YANG Patch has seven operations, aligned with the NETCONF edit operations but with some additions. merge, replace, create, delete and remove mean exactly what the operation attribute means in Section 7.2 of RFC 6241. insert and move are for lists and leaf-lists that are ordered-by user.

The key difference between delete and remove is what happens to a missing item: delete returns an error, remove does not. With create, the target names the node to create, not its parent. A move needs no value.

Conceptually, the first edit is applied to a copy of the target datastore, and each later edit is applied to the result of the earlier ones. After all edits succeed, the result is validated against the YANG constraints, and only then does the server try to apply it. A constraint violation can come from any node in the datastore, including nodes not in the edit list, and MUST be reported.
sections.eli5: Think of building with blocks on a practice table first. You follow your list step by step, check that the finished tower is sound, and only then copy it to the real table.

sections.title: Status Responses and Errors
sections.content:
The server answers with a yang-patch-status message that repeats the patch-id. If everything worked, the server MUST return it with the global status set to ok. A server MAY then omit the per-edit edit-status container.

When something fails, the server SHOULD return a yang-patch-status. Global errors unrelated to a specific edit go in the global-errors case. Per-edit results are listed by edit-id, each either ok or a list of errors with an error-type, error-tag and optional error-app-tag, error-path, error-message and error-info. Edits skipped or not reached get no entry. If a request is rejected before the edits are processed, for instance in a distributed implementation, the server MUST send the appropriate HTTP error response instead.

A server that supports the media type MUST list the :yang-patch capability in the capability leaf-list of the ietf-restconf-monitoring module from RFC 8040.
sections.eli5: After the job, you get a report card. It says the whole thing worked, or it points to the exact line on your list that went wrong.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content:
RFC 8072 registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-patch and the YANG module ietf-yang-patch (prefix ypatch, revision 2017-02-22). The module is conceptual: its definitions give a normative syntax for XML and JSON messages and are not meant to be implemented as datastore contents.

It also registers the two media types, application/yang-patch+xml and application/yang-patch+json. Both are 8-bit, always use utf-8, and list their intended usage as COMMON. The JSON type follows RFC 7951, with metadata handled as in RFC 7952. Finally, it adds the capability identifier urn:ietf:params:restconf:capability:yang-patch:1.0, indexed as :yang-patch.
sections.eli5: The document gets its names and labels officially written into the shared list, so everybody uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
YANG Patch does not add significant new threats beyond those in RFC 8040. Message integrity comes from RESTCONF, and there is no extra way to check that a patch has not been altered. Both client and server MUST be authenticated as in Section 2 of RFC 8040.

A PATCH MUST be applied atomically. Servers SHOULD also apply only the fully validated configuration to the underlying system. The RFC warns that an edit list that deleted an interface and then recreated it could disrupt the system if applied step by step. Servers SHOULD also guard against requests that consume excessive memory or other resources.
sections.eli5: All changes happen together or not at all, so nobody can leave your settings half-done. The helper should also make sure nobody gives it a list so huge it gets worn out.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The appendix uses the jukebox module from RFC 8040. In one example, three create edits add songs to an album, but the first song already exists, so edit edit1 fails with the data-exists error tag and the server answers 409 Conflict. The remaining edits are not attempted.

Other examples add two songs successfully, insert song 6 after song 5 in playlist Foo-One, move song 1 after song 3 with no value, and edit three top-level nodes at once by sending the PATCH to /restconf/data with create, merge and replace edits.
sections.eli5: The examples show a music player's song list: adding songs, putting one in a new spot, and what the report looks like when one song is already there.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN YANG PATCH EDIT OPERATIONS

items.label: create
items.desc: Create a new data resource; error if it already exists.

items.label: delete
items.desc: Delete a data resource; error if it does not exist.

items.label: insert
items.desc: Insert a new user-ordered data resource.

items.label: merge
items.desc: Merge the edit value with the target; create it if missing.

items.label: replace
items.desc: Replace the target data resource with the edit value.

items.label: remove
items.desc: Remove a data resource if it exists.
